title: Cache Stampede: The Five-Minute Expiry Cliff
businessContext: A product API serves 12000 requests per second. A deployment populated every popular Redis key with the same five-minute TTL. PostgreSQL can sustain only 800 uncached reads per second.
problemStatement: Cache hit rate falls from 98% to 4% in one second; product requests time out across all regions. Work through three timed developments, justify your actions, and write an evidence-based incident response. The simulation starts paused; advancing time can expire unanswered decisions.
constraints: Do not serve stale prices or inventory as authoritative checkout values.
Redis is shared with sessions; avoid destructive global operations.
Protect the database before repopulating the cache.
All telemetry is synthetic. Actions only affect this practice simulation.
candidateTasks: Contain customer impact while preserving evidence and data integrity.
Respond to each new development and explain the selected action.
Cite telemetry supporting the root cause; distinguish observation from inference.
Define a permanent correction, regression coverage, recovery gates, and stakeholder update.

hints: Redis memory is normal while 18000 keys expire together.
Cap origin concurrency, coalesce identical reads and shed excess requests with bounded retry hints.
Apply TTL jitter, refresh-ahead for hot keys, and leases with owner tokens, TTL and safe release.
alternativeApproaches: Use a dedicated refresh queue with deduplication and bounded workers.
Precompute hot catalog views and invalidate them from product-change events while retaining expiry as a safety bound.
commonMistakes: Flushing shared Redis or warming with unlimited concurrency.
Serving stale financial values without an explicit correctness policy.
Using a refresh lock without expiration or owner-safe release.
